reference.source: Standard haematopoietic cell transplantation reference texts
clinicalPearls: A clinical syndrome occurring around the time of neutrophil recovery after haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, particularly in autologous transplants
The cardinal features are non-infective fever, an erythematous skin rash, and increased capillary permeability
Capillary leak manifests as weight gain, oedema, and non-cardiogenic pulmonary infiltrates with hypoxaemia
It typically develops within a few days of neutrophil engraftment as recovering cells release inflammatory mediators
It is a diagnosis of exclusion, so infection and other causes of fever during the recovery period must be considered first
It overlaps clinically with early acute graft-versus-host disease in allogeneic transplantation, and the two can be difficult to distinguish
It responds promptly, often dramatically, to a short course of corticosteroids
Severe cases can progress to respiratory failure and multi-organ involvement if untreated
reference.pathophysiology: During neutrophil recovery, a surge of pro-inflammatory cytokines together with newly recovering and activated leucocytes injures the vascular endothelium and increases capillary permeability. The resulting fluid shifts produce oedema, weight gain, and non-cardiogenic pulmonary infiltrates. Because the syndrome occurs in the autologous setting, it is not driven by donor-versus-host alloreactivity, although in allogeneic recipients it overlaps mechanistically and clinically with early acute graft-versus-host disease.
additionalDifferentials: Viral infection such as respiratory viruses or cytomegalovirus
Acute graft-versus-host disease in allogeneic transplantation
Drug reaction, including to growth factors or antimicrobials
Transfusion reaction or fluid overload with cardiogenic pulmonary oedema
additionalInvestigations: Full septic screen including blood and targeted cultures to exclude infection
Chest imaging to characterise non-cardiogenic pulmonary infiltrates
Full blood count documenting neutrophil recovery and inflammatory markers
Assessment of fluid balance and weight change for capillary leak
Echocardiography if a cardiogenic cause of pulmonary oedema is possible
Viral and fungal studies as clinically indicated
redFlags: Attributing fever to the syndrome before serious infection has been excluded
reference.prognosis: The syndrome usually responds rapidly to corticosteroids with good recovery, but severe capillary leak with respiratory failure can be life-threatening and may be associated with a higher rate of transplant-related complications.
pitfalls: Labelling the illness as engraftment syndrome before adequately excluding infection
Delaying corticosteroids in a deteriorating patient
Confusing it with early acute graft-versus-host disease in allogeneic recipients
Attributing pulmonary infiltrates solely to fluid overload
references: Consensus diagnostic criteria for engraftment syndrome
Standard haematopoietic cell transplantation reference texts
management: Treat with systemic corticosteroids as first-line therapy, to which the syndrome usually responds rapidly
Exclude infection first with a full septic screen, as this is a diagnosis of exclusion during neutrophil recovery, covering empirically with antimicrobials until infection is ruled out
Provide supportive care for capillary leak, including judicious fluid management, supplemental oxygen and respiratory support for non-cardiogenic pulmonary infiltrates
Monitor fluid balance, weight and oxygenation closely for evolving capillary-leak syndrome
Escalate to intensive care and ventilatory support in severe capillary leak with respiratory failure
Distinguish from and manage overlapping early acute graft-versus-host disease in allogeneic recipients
Manage within the haematology and transplant team with continued monitoring for transplant-related complications
